question: A 76-year-old male with a history of chronic uncontrolled hypertension presents to the emergency room following an episode of syncope. He reports that he felt lightheaded and experienced chest pain while walking his dog earlier in the morning. He notes that he has experienced multiple similar episodes over the past year. A trans-esophageal echocardiogram demonstrates a thickened, calcified aortic valve with left ventricular hypertrophy. Which of the following heart sounds would likely be heard on auscultation of this patient?

options.opa: Diastolic rumble following an opening snap with an accentuated S1
options.opb: Early diastolic high-pitched blowing decrescendo murmur that is loudest at the left sternal border
options.opc: Crescendo-decrescendo murmur radiating to the carotids that is loudest at the right upper sternal border
options.opd: Holosystolic murmur radiating to the axilla that is loudest at the apex
options.ope: Midsystolic click that is most prominent that is loudest at the apex

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Calcified aortic valve with left ventricular hypertrophy -> Turbulent blood flow through the stenotic valve -> Murmur generation -> 95% CHAIN: Thickened aortic valve -> Increased resistance to blood flow -> Turbulent blood flow -> Murmur generation -> 90% CHAIN: Left ventricular hypertrophy -> Impaired relaxation of the left ventricle -> Diastolic dysfunction -> 85% CHAIN: Aortic valve calcification -> Reduced valve mobility -> Turbulent blood flow -> Murmur generation -> 95%
analysis: The patient's presentation with syncope, chest pain, history of chronic uncontrolled hypertension, and findings of a thickened, calcified aortic valve with left ventricular hypertrophy suggest aortic stenosis. The characteristic heart sound associated with aortic stenosis is a systolic ejection murmur that is crescendo-decrescendo in nature and radiates to the carotids, typically loudest at the right upper sternal border.
